name: linecast
desc: Weather, tides, the sun, the moon, and maps, drawn for the terminal
why: Draws tides, sun and moon positions as terminal line art; a neat transform of astronomical data, though possibly more pretty than deep.

brief.what_it_is: linecast is a set of seven live terminal apps, run as subcommands: weather, sunshine, moon, sky, tides, radar, and maps. Each one draws its view as terminal line art from free public data, with no accounts or API keys. Input is mostly a location, which is saved with `linecast location` or passed with `--location`, plus the current time. Output is a live full-screen view, or a static frame with `--print`. Several apps also offer `--json` for raw data and `--oneline` for a status bar. The project is Python, and the README says it runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows, over SSH, and in tmux.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as "The Old Farmer's Almanac meets Minitel", with a photo of a 1990s Minitel terminal showing a weather screen as its prior art. The stated idea is to bring weather, tides, sun, moon, sky, and maps into the terminal as drawn charts rather than text tables.
brief.how_it_works: Each subcommand fetches free public data (weather, tide gauges and predictions, radar, map tiles, astronomical positions) and renders it with terminal drawing. Colors are taken from the terminal's own color scheme, and the app redraws when the scheme changes; inside tmux this needs tmux 3.6 or newer, otherwise a fixed palette is used. Where real radar is not published openly, a precipitation model fills in. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: `uv tool install linecast`, `uvx linecast weather` (no install), `pipx` or `pip`, a curl one-line script, or community packages in the AUR and nixpkgs. Needs Python 3.10 or newer. On Windows, use Windows Terminal. A portable option is downloading linecast.pyz from the latest GitHub release and running it with python3, optionally chmod +x and put on PATH as linecast. The portable copy checks weekly for a newer release. No accounts or API keys are required. Optional: a TideCheck key for more tide stations, set through environment variables (see docs/configuration.md). Shell completion via `source <(linecast completion zsh)` (bash, zsh, fish, nu are supported). Without a saved location, it guesses from IP address.
brief.standout: Instead of tables, it draws charts in the terminal: a weather year laid out the way Tufte drew New York's, a sky view that can lie back until the horizon becomes a circle with the whole sky inside it, and a tide view that breaks the tide into sun and moon components. Colors follow the user's terminal theme, and there are sky cultures and traditional calendars and hours (Hawaiian, Chinese, Hebrew, Islamic, and others) built in.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release date, changelog, or last-commit date. Visible evidence: a Tests workflow badge, a PyPI badge pointing to pypi.org/project/linecast, and a Terminal Trove Tool of the Week badge. The README describes a substantial and recently extended feature set, including multiple languages and 22 sky cultures, but I did not check the commit history or release page to confirm activity.
brief.caveats: Windows needs Windows Terminal. Inside tmux, theme colors need tmux 3.6 or newer, or it falls back to a fixed palette. Real radar covers only North America, Europe, and parts of East and Southeast Asia; elsewhere the view shows a model. Tide sources are strongest in the US, Canada, Queensland, Hong Kong, Japan, and Norway, with about 1,200 extra gauges and global predictions elsewhere. The year and makeup tide views need a source with year-round predictions. Location guessed from IP can be far off on a VPN or over SSH. Persian, Hebrew, and Arabic are marked experimental and need native-speaker review; Persian does not display well in macOS Terminal or iTerm2. Month, year, and tide makeup views with --print have no --json, --oneline, or --prose output. The README says nothing about licensing beyond MIT, which is listed in the License section and the badge. The homepage fetch did not reach the docs, so details in docs/ are unverified.
